text: You've spent seven chapters learning how networks and attacks work on paper. A SOC analyst's real job is almost entirely hands-on: staring at real traffic, recognizing a real pattern, and reacting under real time pressure. A home lab — a small, isolated set of virtual machines running on one computer — is how you get that practice for free, without needing a job, a corporate network, or anyone's permission but your own.

A useful first lab needs four free pieces. A hypervisor, VirtualBox or VMware Workstation Player, is the software that runs your virtual machines on one physical computer. Kali Linux is your attacker VM, pre-loaded with the tools this course has already referenced — Nmap, Wireshark, Metasploit. Metasploitable2 is a deliberately vulnerable target VM from Rapid7, built on purpose to be exploited legally. And pfSense, optional, gives you a real open-source virtual firewall to write your own rules on.

The setup step that actually matters is network isolation. Every hypervisor lets you choose how a VM connects. Set each lab VM's network adapter to Host-Only in VirtualBox, or Internal Network in VMware — never Bridged, which would expose live exploit traffic directly to your real home network and the internet. An isolated virtual network means your Kali VM scanning your Metasploitable2 VM stays entirely inside your laptop, with nothing leaking out and nothing able to reach in.

Take a snapshot before you try anything risky, so a broken VM is one click from fixed. And remember this platform's own guidance about subscribing to a structured lab service like TryHackMe — that pairs perfectly with a home lab you fully control yourself. Just hold onto the one rule: only ever attack systems you own or have explicit written authorization to test. Same tools, same actions — authorization is the only thing that makes it legal.
With a lab up and isolated, you're ready to actually look at traffic. Next up: Wireshark — capturing live packets and reading what's really happening inside them.
